clue.text: Crazy to use two drugs

parts.note: crack is a form of cocaine
pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Someone argues it would be mad to take two drugs at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two drugs' supplies both halves: CRACK (cocaine) and POT (cannabis), side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A crackpot is an eccentric person with mad ideas, and the word works as an adjective meaning crazy.

clue.text: Another chance to see the fleet outside ebbing river

indicators.note: the fleet's letters sit outside, wrapping round the river piece

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, Britain's fleet

indicators.note: an ebbing tide flows back, so the river's name is read backwards

parts.note: the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Naval ships sit at the river mouth as the tide goes out, a second viewing for onlookers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ebbing' turns URE into ERU, and 'outside' puts R...N round it. The Ure is a Yorkshire river, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: A repeat broadcast of a programme gives viewers a second opportunity to watch it.

clue.text: Little money, near exhausted, Ian is a very senior citizen

parts.note: a cent is a coin of small value

indicators.note: something exhausted is worn out and disordered, so the word near is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pensioner called Ian is almost out of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exhausted' looks like 'near broke' but rearranges NEAR into ENAR, between CENT and IAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has reached the age of a hundred is certainly an elderly person.

clue.text: Rules that voting system expects to change, having lost vote

parts.note: PR is proportional representation, an electoral system

indicators.note: the remaining letters of expects are to change their order
the word expects loses the mark that stands for a vote

parts.note: X is the mark a voter puts on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A political note that proportional representation would alter the rules after a lost ballot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost' takes X out of EXPECTS, leaving EPECTS, which 'to change' rearranges to ECEPTS after PR.
explanation.definitionFit: Precepts are principles laying down how to behave, that is, guiding rules.

clue.text: Railway official with masses of parking offences

explanation.surface: A railway employee turns out to have a pile of unpaid parking fines.
explanation.definitionFit: On a train, the staff member who checks passes collects them; a driver piling up parking fines is, humorously, a collector of such slips too.

clue.text: Sly flyers replace one in built up area

indicators.note: the flyers take the place of the letter that stands for one, inside the built-up area

parts.note: a city is a large built-up area
the RAF is the Royal Air Force, Britain's flyers

explanation.surface: Sneaky airmen take over a spot in the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is the Roman numeral I; 'replace one in' swaps the I of CITY for RAF.
explanation.definitionFit: Crafty and sly both describe someone cunning who gets their way by deceit.

clue.text: State sea at Nice, say, is less rough

parts.note: Cal. is an abbreviation for the US state of California
mer is French for sea, as spoken in Nice

explanation.surface: Seemingly a remark that the Riviera's waters are less choppy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' is the French Riviera city, not the adjective, so the sea is in French: MER, after CAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea that is quieter or more tranquil is less rough.

clue.text: First class! First rate broadcast!

parts.note: A1 means first-class, with the 1 read as the letter I

indicators.note: the opening letter of rate is taken

explanation.surface: An excited cry praising something top-notch.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first class) is written AI, the digit read as I; 'First' then takes R from 'rate'.
explanation.definitionFit: To air a programme or opinion is to put it out publicly, to transmit it.

clue.text: He spreads stories around and speculates

indicators.note: spreading the words about scatters their letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A gossip passes tales around while guessing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spreads ... around' signals the anagram of HE and STORIES; 'around' only reinforces it.
explanation.definitionFit: To theorise is to form ideas or hypotheses, much as to speculate is to conjecture.

clue.text: British and French eleven given medal

parts.note: onze is French for eleven

explanation.surface: An Anglo-French football side wins third place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eleven' sounds like a team but is the number, in French: ONZE.
explanation.definitionFit: Bronze is the third-place award at the Olympics and other contests.

clue.text: Close air circuit for measurements of heat

indicators.note: going round a circuit sends the letters round into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A stuffy closed-loop air system and its heat readings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circuit' reorders CLOSE AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A calorie is a unit of energy, used to quantify heat.

clue.text: Eke out new ingredient for joint

indicators.note: the new letter goes in as an ingredient, mixed into the middle
out here means put out of order, so the word eke is rearranged

explanation.surface: A cook stretches a dish with a fresh addition for the roast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges EKE as KEE, and 'ingredient' puts N inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The knee is the hinge where thigh meets lower leg, a body joint.

clue.text: Simple novel remark to doctor

explanation.surface: A fictional detective's famous line to his medical friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the line popularly credited to Sherlock Holmes, 'Elementary, my dear Watson', said to Dr Watson in the stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary means basic or easy; it is also the word Holmes is famed for addressing to Dr Watson.

clue.text: Instrument for surveying how the cat got hurt inside blasted tree

indicators.note: the pain word goes inside the cat word

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
to ache is to hurt, to feel pain

indicators.note: a blasted tree is shattered, so its letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A surveyor's tool is described via a cat injured in a lightning-struck tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts ACHE in TOM for TACHEOM; 'blasted' turns TREE into ETER at the end. 'how' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tacheometer is a theodolite used to measure distances and heights quickly in land surveys.

clue.text: Festive occasion with court in charge of all the stars

parts.note: a gala is a festive celebration

explanation.surface: A celebrity party at court where the guest list is all stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all the stars' hints at celebrities but means the galaxy.
explanation.definitionFit: Galactic means relating to a galaxy, the vast system of stars.

clue.text: Theoretical society of dons

parts.note: academic can mean theoretical, not practical

explanation.surface: Seemingly a learned college society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' is the noun (university teachers), not the verb 'puts on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dons are university teachers, scholars working in higher education.

clue.text: Ready? But Charlie has to change

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: the word has is to change, so its letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A question of whether Charlie is prepared, and whether he has to alter something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is a noun here, old slang for money. 'to change' reorders HAS as ASH after C.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready (or readies) is British slang for money in notes and coins.

clue.text: Interbreeding, just part of his sign is sorcerer's comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the run of letters is read in reverse
only a portion of the letters of these words is used

explanation.surface: A wizard's astrological sign is said to be making a return.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'siGN IS SORCerer's' sits GNISSORC; 'comeback' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossing is mating two breeds or varieties to produce a hybrid.

clue.text: Get ready to take off in a cab

explanation.surface: An aircraft heads for the runway like a cab.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane taxis along the ground before take-off; a taxi is also a hired car, so to taxi is to ride in one.

clue.text: First Lady greases wheels with her bounty

indicators.note: the opening letter of Lady is taken
wheels as a verb means turns round, so the letters of greases are spun into a new order

explanation.surface: A president's wife oils the wheels of government with her generosity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' looks like a president's wife but gives only L; 'wheels' rearranges GREASES.
explanation.definitionFit: Largesse is generous giving of gifts or money, a liberal bounty.

clue.text: Covers songs for two, very inclusive

indicators.note: the duets include the extra letter within them

parts.note: duets are songs for two performers

explanation.surface: A singing duo's cover versions take in a great many songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' suggests cover versions of songs, but means bedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Duvets are quilts that cover a bed, also called continental quilts.

clue.text: They take the risk again

parts.note: reads like gamblers trying once more, but describes firms that underwrite insurance already held by other insurers

explanation.surface: Daredevils go back for another dangerous attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Reinsurance firms accept part of a risk that an insurance company has already covered, taking it on a second time.

clue.text: Savage hit back outside university

indicators.note: the reversed hit sits outside, around the university letter
back means the word for hit is reversed

parts.note: to lam is to beat or hit

explanation.surface: A violent student strikes back outside the campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LAM into MAL, which goes round U.
explanation.definitionFit: To maul is to attack and wound fiercely, as a wild animal savages its prey.

clue.text: New clue? New, but relative

indicators.note: new here means renewed, so the letters of the clue word are freshly arranged

explanation.surface: A puzzle-setter submits a fresh clue but its source is relative.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'New' rearranges CLUE with N, from the second 'New'.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncle is a family member, the brother of a parent.

clue.text: One chap on the back cover shown to be working hard

indicators.note: the remaining pieces come on, that is after, the reversed cover
on the back means the cover word is turned round

parts.note: a lid is a cover
I is the Roman numeral for one
gent is short for gentleman, a chap

explanation.surface: A man pictured on a book's back cover is shown hard at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses LID as DIL; 'on' places I and GENT after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone diligent is industrious, careful and persistent in effort.

clue.text: I will shortly become poorly

parts.note: will is shortened to the 'll of a contraction; that these letters also sit inside the word is a coincidence

explanation.surface: Someone predicts that they will soon fall sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I will' contracts to I'LL; 'shortly' signals the short form.
explanation.definitionFit: Poorly is British usage for unwell or sick.

clue.text: Can't it be repaired? Made whole?

indicators.note: something repaired is fixed by putting its parts together anew, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A worried owner asks whether a broken item can be mended and restored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be repaired' rearranges CANT and IT; the apostrophe is not a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Intact means undamaged and complete, like something restored to wholeness.

clue.text: Pals working at writing songs

indicators.note: working here means being worked over, so the letters of pals are rearranged

parts.note: MS stands for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Friends work together writing songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges PALS as PSAL, then MS (manuscript) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalms are sacred songs, especially those in the biblical Book of Psalms.

clue.text: Looked at king for example with terrible dread

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king
e.g. is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example

indicators.note: terrible means dreadfully wrong, so the letters of dread are jumbled

explanation.surface: A monarch was eyed with fearful dread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' rearranges DREAD as ARDED after R and EG.
explanation.definitionFit: Regarded means looked at attentively, gazed upon or considered.
